column1: # image-cap-cases.tsv — THE truth table for the theme-bundle image size caps,
# and the only copy of those four numbers.
# WHY THIS FILE EXISTS
# The image gate is implemented TWICE, in two languages, with no compiler
# between them:
#   server/ocserverd/avatar_bundle.go    validImageValue    — the AUTHORITY. It
#                                        is what actually refuses a write (422).
#   frontend/src/lib/themeBundleCore.ts  isValidImageValue  — the cockpit's copy,
#                                        so a picked file is refused at the file
#                                        picker instead of after a round trip.
# Before T-72da there was ONE pair of caps and the only thing tying the two
# implementations together was two hand-written comments saying "the twin of"
# each other. A comment is not a gate. T-72da then split the caps per purpose,
# which doubled the number of loose numbers from two to four — so the twinning
# is now checked rather than asserted in prose.
# A drift produces no error anywhere. It produces one of two silent lies:
#   - cockpit cap LOWER than the server's  → the owner picks a perfectly good
#     background and the cockpit says "invalid image"; the server would have
#     taken it. The failure is invisible from the server side.
#   - cockpit cap HIGHER than the server's → the cockpit accepts the file, puts
#     it in the bundle, and the save 422s later with a message about a file the
#     owner already believed was fine.
# So both sides are checked against THIS table rather than against each other.
# A mock of one side inside the other's test proves only that the mock agrees
# with itself; the table is the shared truth, and a drift NAMES THE SIDE that
# drifted. This is the same shape as bin/tests/fixtures/doc-cap-cases.tsv.
#   server/ocserverd/image_cap_mirror_test.go   the Go half
#   frontend/src/lib/imageCap.test.ts           the TS half
# THE RULE
# Two caps per purpose: the DECODED byte size, and the raw data-URI string
# length (a cheap pre-filter that runs BEFORE the base64 decode). base64
# inflates ~4/3, so each value-len cap sits above its decoded cap × 4/3 with
# margin.
# The two purposes have DELIBERATELY DIFFERENT numbers and must not be tidied
# back into one:
#   avatar   64 KiB — avatars / logo / navIcons are 30-40px glyphs in a roster
#                     row, the top bar, or a tab. Nothing legitimate needs more,
#                     and this is the real guard against bloating a theme. (It
#                     said "the single custom_themes JSON row" until T-83ef gave
#                     themes their own table — one row each now, so the cap
#                     bounds what ONE theme weighs rather than what one shared
#                     row does. The number and the reason for it are unchanged.)
#   background 512 KiB — backgrounds.canvas is stretched or tiled across the
#                     WHOLE viewport. At 64 KiB the owner's real background read
#                     as visibly blurry; he reported it three times. Owner ruling
#                     2026-08-03, which overturned the T-081b decision that a
#                     background must share the avatar cap. That decision's
#                     premise was that both went through ONE gate, so relaxing
#                     the background would have relaxed the avatar too — which
#                     is exactly what the per-purpose split removes.
# The caps are read from the four `# <name><TAB><n>` lines below, so neither
# implementation's constant is a third copy of itself.
# 🔴 THE VALUE-LEN CAPS ARE NOT INDEPENDENTLY OBSERVABLE FROM THE OUTSIDE, and
# that is why they are on the table as declared numbers rather than as rows. A
# data URI long enough to trip the value-len cap while carrying a VALID image
# would decode to more than the decoded cap, so the decoded cap would refuse it
# anyway; the pre-filter only ever changes WHICH error you get, never whether
# you get one. It is defence in depth (refuse a pathological string before
# allocating its decode), not a separate behaviour. What the rows below DO prove
# about it is the direction that actually broke things: the `background-at-cap`
# row can only pass if the background value-len cap moved with the decoded cap —
# 512 KiB decoded is ~683 KiB encoded, so a value-len left at the avatar's
# 96 KiB rejects it as "too long" and the decoded cap is never reached.
# cap declarations, read by both halves:
# avatar_bytes
# avatar_value_len
# background_bytes
# background_value_len
# COLUMNS  case<TAB>purpose<TAB>decoded_bytes<TAB>accepted
#   case           row name, used in failure messages
#   purpose        avatar | logo | navicon | background — selects WHICH bundle
#                  field the value is fed through. Both halves drive the real
#                  validate* entry point for that field, not the bare gate, so a
#                  cap that is raised but wired to the wrong call site still
#                  fails here.
#   decoded_bytes  size of the decoded PNG (a real 8-byte PNG signature followed
#                  by zero padding — the magic-byte check is orthogonal to size
#                  and must keep passing, or a row would go red for the wrong
#                  reason)
#   accepted       expected verdict: true = the field admits this value
